slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 16: Selecting Standard Library Containers. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

slides.title: 16.1.2 Evaluating Insertion and Access Costs
keyPoints: List insertion at an already known valid position can avoid shifting later elements, but locating that position.
Vector insertion in the middle moves later elements, while appending can be amortized constant time across growth.
Count lookup, allocation, element movement, and subsequent traversal together.
List insertion at an already known valid position can avoid shifting later elements, but locating that position.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 16, treat 16.1.2 Evaluating Insertion and Access Costs as a design decision with costs and evidence. List insertion at an already known valid position can avoid shifting later elements, but locating that position may require linear traversal. Vector insertion in the middle moves later elements, while appending can be amortized constant time across growth. Count lookup, allocation, element movement, and subsequent traversal together. Stable references can justify a node-based structure even when raw traversal is slower. Conversely, a dense read-heavy workload often benefits from contiguous storage. Use complexity to eliminate obviously unsuitable designs, then benchmark representative complete operations rather than an isolated instruction chosen to favor one container. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: 16.2.2 Comparing Hash-Based Containers
keyPoints: An unordered map uses a hash to organize candidate locations and equality to decide key matches.
Equal keys must produce compatible hash values under the container’s requirements.
Average constant-time lookup depends on hashing and workload conditions; worst-case behavior can be linear.
Iteration order is not a sorted-order contract and may change after rehashing or between implementations.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 16, treat 16.2.2 Comparing Hash-Based Containers as a design decision with costs and evidence. An unordered map uses a hash to organize candidate locations and equality to decide key matches. Equal keys must produce compatible hash values under the container’s requirements. Average constant-time lookup depends on hashing and workload conditions; worst-case behavior can be linear. Iteration order is not a sorted-order contract and may change after rehashing or between implementations. Rehashing also has iterator consequences distinct from element-reference rules. Use an ordered container or sort a separate result when output order is a requirement. Reserve and load-factor tuning can reduce avoidable rehashing but do not repair a poor or adversarial hash policy. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 16, treat Match each container to one observable property as a design decision with costs and evidence. The deque demonstrates insertion at both ends. The lists demonstrate node transfer with a retained iterator to a moved element. The ordered map demonstrates key order, while the unordered map demonstrates equivalent lookup by key without a required iteration order. The set demonstrates uniqueness. These are separate mechanisms, not a benchmark ranking the containers. The retained list iterator refers to an element moved into the destination list by splice. The element survives; ownership by the containing list changes. That is different from copying the element into a new node and erasing the old node. The example’s iterator check is meaningful because the selected operation provides the relevant preservation guarantee. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 16, treat Failure clinic — A report inherited hash order as a design decision with costs and evidence. An application prints an unordered map directly and stores the output as a golden fixture. A later library or capacity change reorders the lines, and the test reports a regression even though the logical records are unchanged. Either output order is not part of the contract, in which case the test should compare unordered content, or deterministic output is required, in which case the implementation needs an explicit ordering stage. Another defect uses counts[name] to check whether a name exists. Missing names are inserted with zero counts, changing the dataset during inspection. Use an absence-preserving query when the operation is read-only. A third defect compares list insertion with vector insertion while excluding the list’s position search. That measurement answers a narrower question than the advertised workload. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 16, treat Guided lab — Separate ownership from indexes as a design decision with costs and evidence. Design a small catalog that owns records in a vector and builds an ID index for lookup. Decide whether the index stores positions, stable IDs, or copies. If it stores positions, rebuild or update it whenever mutations can change positions. Test that a failed duplicate-ID load leaves the previous catalog and its index consistent. Compare an ordered and unordered index using the same accepted records. Verify lookup results and missing-key behavior. Generate report output through an explicitly sorted snapshot so both storage choices produce the same public order. This demonstrates that a storage optimization need not redefine presentation semantics.
